Title: Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization
Abstract: We present the problem of approximating the time-evolution operator e^{-i\hat{H}t} to error \epsilon, where the Hamiltonian \hat{H}=(\langle G|\otimes\hat{\mathcal{I}})\hat{U}(|G\rangle\otimes\hat{\mathcal{I}}) is the projection of a unitary oracle \hat{U} onto the state |G\rangle created by another unitary oracle. Our algorithm solves this with a query complexity \mathcal{O}\big(t+\log({1/\epsilon})\big) to both oracles that is optimal with respect to all parameters in both the asymptotic and non-asymptotic regime, and also with low overhead, using at most two additional ancilla qubits. This approach to Hamiltonian simulation subsumes important prior art considering Hamiltonians which are d-sparse or a linear combination of unitaries, leading to significant improvements in space and gate complexity, such as a quadratic speed-up for precision simulations. It also motivates useful new instances, such as where \hat{H} is a density matrix. A key technical result is `qubitization', which uses the controlled version of these oracles to embed any \hat{H} in an invariant \text{SU}(2) subspace. A large class of operator functions of \hat{H} can then be computed with optimal query complexity, of which e^{-i\hat{H}t} is a special case.

Title: Optimal Hamiltonian Simulation by Quantum Signal Processing
Abstract: The physics of quantum mechanics is the inspiration for, and underlies, computation. As such, one expects physical intuition to be highly influential in understanding design many algorithms, particularly simulation systems. Surprisingly, this has been challenging, with current Hamiltonian algorithms remaining abstract often result sophisticated but unintuitive constructions. This connection made through general three-step ``quantum signal processing'' methodology, comprised (i) transducing eigenvalues into single ancilla qubit, (ii) transforming these optimal-length sequence rotations, (iii) projecting near unity success probability.

gold.abstract: Quantum signal processing (QSP) and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) have provided a unified framework for understanding many quantum algorithms, including factorization, matrix inversion, and Hamiltonian simulation. As a multivariable version of QSP, multivariable quantum signal processing (M-QSP) is proposed. M-QSP interleaves signal operators corresponding to each variable with signal processing operators, which provides an efficient means to perform multivariable polynomial transformations. However, the necessary and sufficient condition for what types of polynomials can be constructed by M-QSP is unknown. In this paper, we propose a classical algorithm to determine whether a given pair of multivariable Laurent polynomials can be implemented by M-QSP, which returns True or False. As one of the most important properties of this algorithm, it returning True is the necessary and sufficient condition. The proposed classical algorithm runs in polynomial time in the number of variables and signal operators. Our algorithm also provides a constructive method to select the necessary parameters for implementing M-QSP. These findings offer valuable insights for identifying practical applications of M-QSP.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
- QSP’s eigenvalue transduction (step i) can encode spectral properties of a Hamiltonian into ancilla qubit phases. This phase-encoding can be repurposed as a feature map for classical machine learning models, specifically kernel methods. - Method: For a family of 1D spin-1/2 Hamiltonians with varying interaction strengths, compute QSP phase features by simulating short-time evolution on a classical computer (using exact diagonalization for small systems). Use these features to train a support vector machine (SVM) with a radial basis function kernel to classify gapped vs. gapless phases.
- Validation: Compare classification accuracy and sample complexity against SVMs using raw Hamiltonian matrix elements or two-point correlation functions. Use cross-validation on Hamiltonians not seen during training. Benchmark against known phase diagrams from density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations.
- Missing cross-paper knowledge: No second paper is available; integration currently only uses paper-c. A paper on classical kernel methods or quantum phase classification would be needed to ground the SVM design and baseline.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose using quantum signal processing (QSP) to extract spectral phase features from many-body Hamiltonians for classical kernel-based phase classification. QSP’s optimal simulation routine encodes eigenvalues into single-qubit rotation angles, which we use as inputs to a support vector machine. We hypothesize that these features capture non-local spectral information that improves discrimination between gapped and gapless quantum phases compared to local observables. We will test this on 1D spin chains, validating against DMRG phase boundaries. This work bridges quantum algorithm design and quantum matter classification, showing that simulation subroutines can serve as feature extractors for machine learning.

FINAL IDEA: QSP-derived phase features from optimal Hamiltonian simulation can enhance classical kernel methods for classifying quantum phases, linking quantum algorithmic efficiency to improved data representation in many-body physics.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper A (cognitive science): Provides a dual-process account where intuitive (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) processing interact under cognitive load, with measurable shifts in response confidence and error patterns.
- Paper B (behavioral ecology): Provides optimal foraging theory, specifically patch-leaving rules based on diminishing returns and environmental variability, with quantitative predictions for when an agent should switch patches.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Patch-leaving decisions can be modeled as a dual-process trade-off: Type 1 heuristics (e.g., “leave when intake drops below a threshold”) versus Type 2 calculation of marginal value theorem. Cognitive load should bias foragers toward the heuristic, causing predictable deviations from optimal patch residence times—especially in high-variability environments where Type 2 recalculation is most valuable.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
- Participants: 120 adults in a computerized foraging task.
- Task: Harvest virtual patches with varying depletion rates; manipulate environmental variability (low vs. high) and cognitive load (concurrent digit-span vs. no load).
- Measurements: Patch residence time, switch latency, post-trial confidence ratings, and a post-task Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) to index Type 2 propensity.
- Validation: Compare observed residence times against marginal value theorem predictions; test whether load increases heuristic-like switching and reduces fit to optimality, with larger effects in high-variability patches and among low-CRT participants.
- Missing cross-paper knowledge: No prior data exist on whether foraging heuristics map onto Type 1 processes or whether load effects scale with environmental variability; this is an explicit hypothesis to be tested.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
Optimal foraging theory assumes agents compute patch-leaving times rationally, but cognitive science suggests such decisions often rely on fast heuristics under load. We propose that foraging behavior reflects a dual-process architecture: Type 2 processes approximate marginal value calculations, while Type 1 heuristics dominate under cognitive load. In a virtual patch-leaving task, we predict that load increases premature switching, reduces fit to optimality, and lowers confidence—particularly in high-variability environments. This work bridges behavioral ecology and cognitive science by showing that ecological rationality is constrained by processing architecture, not just information.

FINAL IDEA: Cognitive load shifts foraging from optimal marginal-value calculation to heuristic patch-leaving, with effects amplified in high-variability environments.
